questions.stem: For a projectile moving through air resistance-free space, the horizontal component of its velocity

options.text: becomes zero at the highest point

questions.explanation: Gravity acts vertically only, so there is no horizontal force on the projectile. With no horizontal force there is no horizontal acceleration, and the horizontal velocity component keeps whatever value it had at launch.

distractorRationale.a: Nothing pushes the projectile forwards after launch, so it cannot speed up horizontally
distractorRationale.b: This happens in real air because of drag, but the question specifies no air resistance
distractorRationale.d: It is the VERTICAL component that becomes zero at the top; if the horizontal component also vanished the projectile would stop dead in mid-air

questions.stem: Two identical balls are released from the same height at the same instant. One is simply dropped and the other is thrown horizontally. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They land at the same time but at different places
They land at the same time and in the same place

questions.explanation: Both balls begin with zero vertical velocity and fall under the same acceleration g through the same height, so their vertical motions are identical and the times of fall are equal. The thrown ball also travels horizontally, so it lands further away.

distractorRationale.a: Being thrown forwards gives no downward velocity, so it does not delay the fall
distractorRationale.b: Extra horizontal speed cannot shorten the time of fall, which depends only on height and g
distractorRationale.d: Their landing times match, but the thrown ball drifts forwards at a constant horizontal speed

questions.stem: A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the time of flight. Give your answer in seconds.
questions.explanation: The vertical motion starts from rest, so $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ gives $20 = 5t^2$, hence $t^2 = 4$ and $t = 2\ \text{s}$. The launch speed of 15 m/s is horizontal and plays no part in the timing.

questions.stem: A stone is projected horizontally at 15 m/s from a cliff 20 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate how far from the foot of the cliff it strikes the ground. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: First find the time of fall from the vertical motion: $20 = \frac{1}{2}(10)t^2$ gives $t = 2\ \text{s}$. The horizontal velocity is constant, so the range is $R = ut = 15 \times 2 = 30\ \text{m}$.

questions.stem: A stone is projected from level ground at 40 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum height it reaches is
questions.explanation: The vertical component of the launch velocity is $u\sin 30^{\circ} = 40 \times 0.5 = 20\ \text{m/s}$. At the top the vertical velocity is zero, so $H = \frac{u_y^2}{2g} = \frac{400}{20} = 20\ \text{m}$.

distractorRationale.a: Halved the correct answer, perhaps by using 4g instead of 2g in the denominator
distractorRationale.c: Doubled the correct answer by omitting the factor 2 in 2g
distractorRationale.d: Used the full launch speed of 40 m/s as the vertical component, forgetting to resolve

questions.stem: A ball is kicked from level ground with a speed of 40 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate its total time of flight. Give your answer in seconds.
questions.explanation: Vertical component of launch velocity $= 40\sin 30^{\circ} = 20\ \text{m/s}$. Time of flight $T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g} = \frac{2 \times 20}{10} = 4\ \text{s}$. Half of this, 2 s, is the time to reach the highest point.

questions.stem: For a given launch speed on level ground, the horizontal range of a projectile is greatest when the angle of projection is
questions.explanation: The range is $R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$, which is largest when $\sin 2\theta = 1$, that is when $2\theta = 90^{\circ}$ and $\theta = 45^{\circ}$. This angle gives the best compromise between staying in the air and moving forwards.

distractorRationale.a: Gives good forward speed but too little time in the air
distractorRationale.c: Gives long flight time but too little forward speed; it produces exactly the same range as 30°
distractorRationale.d: Projects the body straight up, so the range is zero

questions.stem: A projectile is fired from level ground at 20 m/s at 45° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate its horizontal range. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: $R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$. Here $2\theta = 90^{\circ}$ so $\sin 2\theta = 1$, giving $R = \frac{20^2 \times 1}{10} = \frac{400}{10} = 40\ \text{m}$. At 45° the range formula reduces neatly to $\frac{u^2}{g}$.

questions.stem: A stone is projected from level ground at 30 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the maximum height it reaches. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: Vertical component $u_y = 30\sin 30^{\circ} = 30 \times 0.5 = 15\ \text{m/s}$. Then $H = \frac{u_y^2}{2g} = \frac{15^2}{2 \times 10} = \frac{225}{20} = 11.25\ \text{m}$. Using the full 30 m/s without resolving would wrongly give 45 m.

questions.stem: An aircraft flying horizontally at 100 m/s at a height of 500 m releases a package. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, calculate the horizontal distance the package travels before hitting the ground. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: The package leaves the aircraft with the aircraft's horizontal velocity and zero vertical velocity. Vertically, $500 = \frac{1}{2}(10)t^2 = 5t^2$, so $t^2 = 100$ and $t = 10\ \text{s}$. Horizontally, $R = 100 \times 10 = 1000\ \text{m}$.

questions.stem: Two stones are projected from level ground with the same speed, one at 30° and the other at 60° to the horizontal. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The 30° stone has the greater range
The 60° stone has the greater range
Both have the same range, but the 60° stone rises higher
Both have the same range and the same maximum height

questions.explanation: Range depends on $\sin 2\theta$, and $\sin 60^{\circ} = \sin 120^{\circ}$, so the two complementary angles give identical ranges. Maximum height depends on $\sin^2\theta$, and since $\sin 60^{\circ} > \sin 30^{\circ}$, the steeper 60° projection rises much higher and stays airborne longer.

distractorRationale.a: Would be true only against an angle greater than 45° that is not complementary to 30°
distractorRationale.b: Confuses greater height and longer flight time with greater range
distractorRationale.d: The ranges match, but maximum height depends on sin²θ, which differs sharply between the two angles

questions.stem: Why can horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile be treated independently?

options.text: Because horizontal motion is affected by gravity.
Because vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion.
Because they occur simultaneously but do not influence each other.
Because horizontal motion has no velocity.

questions.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile can be treated independently because they occur simultaneously without affecting each other. The horizontal motion is uniform, while the vertical motion is influenced by gravity, allowing for separate analysis of each component.

distractorRationale.a: This option is incorrect because horizontal motion is not affected by gravity.
distractorRationale.b: While vertical motion is independent, this statement does not fully explain the independence of both motions.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect as horizontal motion does have velocity.

questions.stem: A ball is projected from a height of 10 m with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 45°. What is the maximum height reached above the launch point?
questions.explanation: To find the maximum height above the launch point, we use the formula H = (v_y^2)/(2g), where v_y is the vertical component of the initial velocity. For a 45° launch, v_y = 20sin(45°) = 14.14 m/s. Thus, H = (14.14^2)/(2*10) = 10 m. The total maximum height is 10 m + 10 m = 20 m, but above the launch point, it is 10 m.

distractorRationale.a: This option only considers the height of the launch point, not the maximum height.
distractorRationale.b: This option incorrectly assumes the maximum height is the same as the launch height.
distractorRationale.d: This option overestimates the maximum height reached by the projectile.
